The Manhattan Project. A secret undertaking by the United States, Britain, and Canada to develop atomic weapons during World War II, lasting from 1942 to 1945. Coordinated by J. Robert Oppenheimer and backed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt, it employed over one hundred thirty thousand people across multiple sites and spent two billion dollars in nineteen forty-five money, producing the first nuclear weapons and reshaping warfare, geopolitics, and morality forever.

Albert Einstein and other immigrant physicists warned the Roosevelt administration that Nazi Germany might develop atomic bombs. The fear of German nuclear weapons—which proved unfounded—drove American commitment to the project. Nuclear fission was discovered in nineteen thirty-eight by Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner, and released enormous energy. Creating a critical mass of fissile material would trigger an explosive chain reaction. Leo Szilard, Enrico Fermi, and others at the University of Chicago created the first controlled nuclear chain reaction in December nineteen forty-two beneath Stagg Field, proving that a bomb was theoretically feasible.

The project established secret facilities across the United States: Los Alamos, New Mexico for bomb design and assembly led by Oppenheimer; Oak Ridge, Tennessee for uranium enrichment; and Hanford, Washington for plutonium production. Oak Ridge employed seventy-five thousand workers. Hanford was a secret city of fifty thousand. The project consumed vast electricity and industrial resources while remaining secret from Congress and the American public. Scientists and engineers from across the world worked under security and secrecy while advancing cutting-edge theoretical physics and often improvising engineering solutions under extreme pressure.

On July sixteenth, nineteen forty-five at Alamogordo, New Mexico, the first atomic bomb—Trinity—exploded in the desert, creating a mushroom cloud rising forty thousand feet and releasing energy equivalent to twenty-two thousand tons of TNT. Oppenheimer, watching the blast, famously quoted the Bhagavad Gita: now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds—a moment of existential reckoning with the weapon he had helped create.

President Harry Truman authorized the use of the bombs against Japan. Little Boy, using uranium two thirty-five, destroyed Hiroshima on August sixth, nineteen forty-five. Fat Man, using plutonium two thirty-nine, destroyed Nagasaki on August ninth, killing over two hundred thousand people immediately and hundreds of thousands more from radiation sickness. The bombs induced Japan's surrender, but their devastating civilian toll horrified many of the scientists involved. Oppenheimer and others became advocates for international control of atomic energy and nuclear disarmament. The project's legacy shaped the Nuclear Age: humanity now possessed the capacity to annihilate itself.
